Recursion is a programming technique where a function calls itself to solve a smaller piece of the same problem.  
Each recursive call works on a reduced input and passes the result back up the chain until a simple, directly solvable case—called the **base case**—is reached.  
When the base case is hit, the function stops calling itself and begins returning values, allowing each previous call to combine its own work with the returned result.  
Think of it like a set of nested Russian dolls: you keep opening a smaller doll (the recursive call) until you reach the tiniest one (the base case), then you re‑assemble them in reverse order.
